title: Drawing Pins
passage:
The noticeboard in the porch of the Denhollow reading room is a metre of cork in a wooden frame, with a jam jar of drawing pins on the ledge beside it that anyone may use. Nobody asks permission. Nothing is signed. What governs it is a rule, unwritten and perfectly well known: on the first Monday of the month, every card without a date on it comes down. The rule ___(1)___ nobody’s feelings. Anything with a price on it gets short ___(2)___, so a card advertising guttering repairs is lucky to see a fortnight, while a card asking for help with the churchyard may stay up all summer. Wilf Braddick, who has held the key since the last caretaker gave it up, does the taking down, and what counts as current is left to his discretion. No one voted for that.

What the board is for takes a while to see. Almost none of it is trade. A ladder wanted for one weekend; a lift to the coast on a Thursday; half a sack of daffodil bulbs going spare; tenors wanted, urgently, by a choir that has four. These are errands too small to be worth arranging any other way, and what makes them possible is not neighbourliness but ___(3)___. A card that draws no reply has not been refused. It has only gone unread, and being unread is something a person can live next door to.

None of it can be checked. Nobody writes down what was asked for, and nobody writes down what came of it, so there is no telling whether the ladder was ever lent. Most of what goes up ___(4)___ to nothing. As a way of running anything it is indefensible on ordinary grounds – unaccountable, unmeasured, and administered by one man with a jam jar. ___(5)___, no one in Denhollow has proposed replacing it, and the cards still go up as they always have. Braddick takes them down once they have begun to look sad. The exception is a typed card offering piano lessons, pinned by a woman who stopped teaching in 2014; it has come through more than a decade of first Mondays untouched, on the grounds that taking it down would be a statement and leaving it up is not.
– Verity Padgham, weekend columnist

questions.rationale: Collocation gap. All four options are present-tense third-person transitive verbs beginning in s-, so the set is POS-uniform and shape-matched. The frame is 'The rule ___ nobody’s feelings', and the fixed English collocation for declining to soften a blow is 'spare someone’s feelings'; negated through 'nobody’s', it says the rule is applied without softening, which is exactly what the surrounding sentences report (a dated card survives, an undated one comes down, and the trade cards are cut short). 'spares' locks. saves = collocation_misfit: 'save' is a near-synonym of 'spare' in other frames ('save someone the trouble', 'save face') and is therefore the strongest lure, but English does not say 'save someone’s feelings'. serves = collocation_misfit: one serves a purpose, an interest or a customer; feelings are not served, and the reading that would make it work ('serves nobody’s interests') requires a noun the frame does not supply. spoils = collocation_misfit: 'spoil' takes a surprise, a child or an evening, and it does not mean 'wound', so 'spoils nobody’s feelings' has no idiomatic reading. Only 'spares' collocates with 'feelings' in this frame.

Collocation gap with a suffix-rhymed -ift noun set (all four are real, common English nouns of the same shape and POS). The frame is 'Anything with a price on it gets short ___', and 'get short shrift' is the fixed idiom for being dealt with quickly and without sympathy. The clause that follows supplies the measurement – a commercial card lasts a fortnight where a parish request lasts a season – so the sense the idiom carries is the one the sentence needs. shift = collocation_misfit: the commonest wrong form of this idiom, and 'shift' is a real noun (a work period, a change), but 'get short shift' is not English. thrift = collocation_misfit: thematically tempting beside 'a price on it', since thrift is about money, yet nothing is ever 'given short thrift'. drift = collocation_misfit: English has 'catch someone’s drift' and 'snow drift'; 'short drift' collocates with nothing. Only 'shrift' completes the idiom the frame demands.

Polarity gap; all four options are abstract -ference nouns, so the set is POS-uniform and fully suffix-rhymed and no option is separable on shape. The frame is contrastive – 'what makes them possible is not neighbourliness but ___' – so the gap must hold something set against neighbourliness, and the two sentences after it say what: a card that draws no reply 'has not been refused', it 'has only gone unread'. Being ignored, not being helped, is what keeps the asking cheap, so 'indifference' locks. deference = polarity_mirror: it is the positive-pole social virtue the skimmer reaches for once 'neighbourliness' has set the register, and it is precisely the wrong pole, because the frame demands a term that opposes neighbourliness rather than a second name for it. interference = collocation and sense misfit: it names an intrusion, and the passage describes neighbours doing nothing at all, so nothing in the following two sentences supports it. inference = sense misfit: it is a term for a step in reasoning and has no bearing on what makes a small favour askable, though its shape sits closest of all to the key. Only 'indifference' survives the contrast the frame sets up.

Collocation gap; four one-syllable c- verbs in the same tense and person, shape-matched throughout. The frame is 'Most of what goes up ___ to nothing', and the preposition is doing the work: 'come to nothing' is the fixed English idiom for an effort that produces no result, and it follows directly from the sentence before it, which says that no one records what was asked for or what came of it. counts = collocation_misfit and the sharpest trap in the set: the real idiom is 'count FOR nothing', so a solver who knows the phrase but not its preposition will take it, and the frame gives 'to'. carries = collocation_misfit: English has 'carry weight' and 'carry the day'; 'carry to nothing' does not exist. cuts = collocation_misfit: 'cut to the chase' and 'cut to the bone' are idioms, but 'cut to nothing' is not a way of saying that something failed. Only 'comes' takes 'to nothing' in this frame.

Connective gap; all four are formal sentence-initial connective adverbs of the same class, and none is separable on register. The sentence before it convicts the arrangement – 'indefensible on ordinary grounds – unaccountable, unmeasured, and administered by one man with a jam jar' – while the gapped sentence reports that the village has not replaced it and that the cards go up as they always have. The two stand against each other, so only a concessive connective fits: 'Nonetheless' locks. Accordingly = wrong_logic and the reading a careless solver will accept: it makes the indictment the reason nobody replaces the board, whereas an indefensible arrangement is a reason TO replace it; the arrow points the wrong way. Furthermore = wrong_logic: it adds a further charge in the same direction, but the clause after the gap is not a charge – 'still go up as they always have' reports the board carrying on undisturbed, which cannot be a second count in the indictment. Correspondingly = wrong_logic: it asserts a matching or proportional relation between the two facts, and no such correspondence is on offer. Only 'Nonetheless' carries the reversal the paragraph turns on.
